page.title: When the actor is not there · tinyactors guides
page.description: What a send does when its actor is hibernated, ended or never spawned, and the three ways an application handles it.

hero.headline: Decide what a send to nobody does.
hero.lede: A send to a hibernated actor wakes it, and a send to no actor fails at once. What happens next is your application's choice, per kind of actor.

section.heading: The host handles three cases.
section.p: A send names an actor that may not be in memory, or may not exist at all. The host's answer depends on which.

item.text: The host keeps the event in its queue and wakes the actor, loading its blob itself when the host has a store. The event runs as if the actor had never left, and a send to a name finds a hibernated actor as it finds a resident one.

item.term: No actor has that name or session.
item.text: It was never spawned, or it ended. The sender gets error.communication at once, in the same run, with the send's sendid; an actor.send or host.send from your program throws StaleError instead.
The send goes to your transport (), and whether it arrives is your transport's to say.

section.p: The package has no fallback for the second case: no queue of undelivered events and no spawn on a miss. An application usually uses three ways, each for its own kind of actor.

section.heading: Keep long-lived actors and let them hibernate.
section.p: An actor that stands for a workspace, a room or an account has no top-level <final>, so it never ends. It is always there to send to by its name.
A host with a store and a resident bound keeps it in memory only while it works. An idle actor costs its blob in your store ().

example.code: the room is in the store: true the room has had 1 messages the room has had 2 messages the room is in the store: true

section.p: The member never learns that the room was hibernated. The host loaded it for the first post and hibernated it again once the turn was done.
Use this way when the set of actors is known and each is worth keeping until it is deleted on purpose. Your program or a collection actor makes them.

section.heading: Route sends through an I/O processor.
section.p: An actor made on demand, or a user who may be offline, gets its sends through an I/O processor instead. The processor looks the actor up with send.host.actor and makes it when it is missing.
It forwards the event with the sender's address as its origin, so the actor answers the sender directly:

example.code: made cart.ada the cart holds 1 the cart holds 2

section.p: The lookup, the spawn and the forward are your program's, so the policy is too. It may refuse instead of spawning, or read the actor's starting state from your database.
It may also queue the event while something else makes the actor.
When rules decide which actors may exist, keep the decision in a chart. A collection actor that never ends checks each request and makes the actors with the package's Spawner.
The processor then only forwards to the collection (Spawning from a chart).
The same way serves what is not an actor. A processor for direct messages forwards to each of the user's open connections, or stores the message when there are none.

section.heading: Let the sender handle error.communication.
section.p: An actor that ends, such as a connection, a job or an order, may get a send after its end. The sender should see that, and gets error.communication with the send's sendid at once.
A transition on it decides what follows: tell the user, retry elsewhere, or give up.
A send to a session that ended, or to a name no actor has, fails this way. A send to another system's address reaches your transport instead.
The transport fails it, with send.fail() or with host.fail from the other side, when it learns the actor is not there.

section.heading: Choose the way by the actor's lifetime.

row.cell: long-lived, a known set (a workspace, a room, an account)
made on demand, or not an actor at all (a cart, a user who may be offline)
direct messages (chat:inbox), rooms made by their workspace
short-lived, ends on its own (a connection, a job)
a join of a room that does not exist

section.p: The chat example uses all three, and its README says where.

section.heading: Name actors with unreserved characters only.
section.p: A name is written into addresses: tinyactors://chat/@<name> in a chart's target, in a processor's lookup, in your logs. An address's name holds only the characters RFC 3986 calls unreserved.
Those are A-Z, a-z, 0-9, -, ., _ and ~, and any other byte is percent-encoded. Core's address grammar checks it.
Address.fromName encodes for you, but room/general is then room%2Fgeneral in every address. A chart that writes the name as it reads is not sending to an address at all:

example.code: tinyactors://chat/@room%2Fgeneral tinyactors://chat/@room.acme.general error.communication for raw tinyactors://chat/#_scxml_1

section.p: Name an actor by its kind and its ids joined by ., each id of lowercase letters, digits and -. Examples are room.acme.general, workspace.acme and cart.ada.
Check an id that comes from a user before it becomes part of a name. The system's own id is stricter: lowercase letters, digits, - and ..
Names with parts also avoid two lookups by other keys. Core finds an unnamed actor by its chart's name, and an invoked child by its invoke id.
So a name room would find any unnamed actor of the chart room, and cart the child of an <invoke id="cart">. room.acme.general equals neither.
A name has one owner, the collection actor that spawns it (Spawning from a chart).

section.heading: Key a table by the origin's fragment.
section.p: A room's members or a workspace's pending requests are tables keyed by _event.origin, the sender's address. Core writes one sender's origin in two forms:

item.text: when the send stayed in the sender's segment of the host: a send to a session's address (#_scxml_<n>, or the full address of a session of the same system), to #_parent, to an invoked child, and a delayed send among them;

when the host routed the send: a send to a name (@room.acme.general), to a session in another segment, or from another system (whatever origin its transport passes, the full address when it passes the sender's origin on).

section.p: Both name the same sender, so key the table by the origin from # on. A chart-level <script> holds the helper, and the expressions call it with the origin:
The fragment is a key and a target too: <send targetexpr="key"> reaches the sender from any segment of the host.

section.heading: Keep the system when senders cross systems.
section.p: A directory that answers several hosts holds senders of other systems, so its keys must keep the system. An origin from another system always names it.
There, complete a fragment with the actor's own system, from its own address in _ioprocessors.scxml.location:
section.code:
<script>
  /** The sender's full address; `self` is _ioprocessors.scxml.location. */
  function senderAddress(origin, self) {
    return origin.startsWith('#_scxml_') ? self.slice(0, self.indexOf('#')) + origin : origin;
  }
</script>
<assign location="members" expr="({ ...members, [senderAddress(_event.origin, _ioprocessors.scxml.location)]: _event.data })"/>
section.p: An event from a service your program runs (invocation.sendBack) has the origin #_<invokeid>. It names that invocation in this actor only, and either helper leaves it as it is.
